name: Endocrine
summary: The endocrine glands release hormones, chemical messengers that travel in the blood and steer growth, metabolism, stress responses, blood sugar, salt and water balance, sleep and reproduction. The hypothalamus in the brain directs the pituitary gland, which in turn directs several of the others.

notShown.name: Hypothalamic nuclei
notShown.note: The clusters of nerve cells inside the hypothalamus that make its hormones, such as the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei. Neither source model separates them, so the hypothalamus is one part.

notShown.name: Pituitary stalk
notShown.note: The thin stalk that hangs the pituitary gland from the hypothalamus and carries its nerve fibres and blood vessels. Neither source model has it as a mesh.

notShown.name: Intermediate lobe of the pituitary
notShown.note: A thin band between the anterior and posterior lobes, very small in adults. Z-Anatomy labels it but has no mesh for it.

notShown.name: Adrenal cortex and medulla
notShown.note: Each adrenal gland has an outer cortex, which makes cortisol, aldosterone and some sex hormones, and an inner medulla, which makes adrenaline and noradrenaline. The models show each gland as one part.

notShown.name: Pancreatic islets
notShown.note: About a million tiny cell clusters scattered through the pancreas, together only 1 to 2% of it. They make insulin and glucagon; the rest of the pancreas makes digestive juice.

notShown.name: Leydig cells
notShown.note: The cells between the sperm-making tubules of each testis that make testosterone.

notShown.name: Paraganglia and carotid bodies
notShown.note: Small clusters of hormone-making cells along the nerves and great vessels, related to the adrenal medulla. Neither source model has them.

notShown.name: Ovaries
notShown.note: The female glands that make oestrogen and progesterone. The models are of one adult male body, so they have none.

notShown.name: Hormone-making cells of the stomach and gut
notShown.note: Cells scattered through the lining of the stomach and intestines that release hormones such as gastrin, ghrelin, secretin and GLP-1. The stomach and intestines are shown in the Digestive layer.

notShown.name: Fat tissue
notShown.note: Body fat releases leptin, which signals how much energy the body has stored. Neither source model has fat as a part.

notShown.name: Kidneys
notShown.note: Besides making urine, they release renin, which helps control blood pressure, erythropoietin, which drives red blood cell production, and the active form of vitamin D.

notShown.name: Heart
notShown.note: Its atria release natriuretic peptides when stretched, which make the kidneys pass more salt and water.

notShown.name: Liver
notShown.note: It makes IGF-1, which carries out much of growth hormone's effect, and hepcidin, which controls iron levels.

hypothalamus.description: The control centre of the hormone system, under the thalamus. It makes hormones that tell the pituitary gland what to release, and makes oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone, which the posterior pituitary stores and releases.

anterior pituitary.description: The front lobe of the pea-sized pituitary gland, which sits in a hollow of the sphenoid bone. It makes growth hormone, prolactin, and the hormones that drive the thyroid, the adrenal glands and the testes.

posterior pituitary.description: The back lobe of the pituitary gland, an extension of the hypothalamus. It releases antidiuretic hormone, which makes the kidneys hold on to water, and oxytocin.

pineal gland.description: A pine-cone-shaped gland, about 8 mm long, deep in the middle of the brain. It releases melatonin in the dark, which helps set the body's sleep-wake rhythm.

thyroid gland.description: A butterfly-shaped gland wrapped around the front of the windpipe, below the larynx. Its hormones, thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), set how fast the body uses energy, and it also makes calcitonin, which can lower blood calcium.

superior parathyroid gland.description: One of four rice-grain-sized glands on the back of the thyroid. They make parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium by drawing it from bone and helping the kidneys and gut hold on to it.

inferior parathyroid gland.description: One of four rice-grain-sized glands on the back of the thyroid, the lower pair. They make parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium by drawing it from bone and helping the kidneys and gut hold on to it.

lobe of thymus.description: One of the two lobes of the thymus, behind the breastbone. Its hormones, such as thymosin, help T cells mature; it is largest in childhood and is mostly replaced by fat in adults.

adrenal gland.description: A small gland on top of each kidney. Its outer layer makes cortisol, the stress and blood sugar hormone, and aldosterone, which keeps salt in the body; its core makes adrenaline and noradrenaline for the fight-or-flight response.

pancreas.description: Besides digestive juice, it makes insulin, which lowers blood sugar, and glucagon, which raises it. Those hormones come from about a million tiny islets of cells scattered through the gland.

testis.description: Besides sperm, each testis makes testosterone, which drives male development, muscle and bone growth, and sperm production. The pituitary's hormones control how much it makes.
